Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Time, the calendar & feasts

festival noun

a day of celebration

also feast day, holy day, festivity

classical

Cato, Agr. 143.2
Cic. Arch. 13: fēstōs diēs lūdōrum
Plaut. Aul. 380–381

1fēstus: long e (Lewis & Short leaves it unmarked). De Vaan 212, s.v. fēriae: fēriae and fēstus rest on *fēs-, “divine, holy”. Ruling: Which authority settles a vowel.

diēs fēstus1

a feast day, a festival

A day kept for the gods, as against a working day, diēs profēstus (Plaut. Aul. 380–381); a festival of several days is diēs fēstī or fēriae. Most Roman festivals are neuter plurals: Sāturnālia, Parīlia.

Other words

  • fēriae, fēriārum f. pl. — a festival; holidays

    noun, first declension, plural · also used · classical · Liv. 41.16.1: Latīnae fēriae; Cic. Off. 3.59: fēriae quaedam piscātōrum

    Days of rest kept for a festival; also the holidays (see holidays).

  • fēstum1, fēstī n. — a feast, a festival

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Ov. F. 4.877 (Lewis & Short)

    (vōx plērumque poētica: Ov.)

    Poetic and late Latin for diēs fēstus (Lewis & Short); in Church Latin a feast of the Church (fēstum nātīvitātis Chrīstī, Traupman 291).

Examples

  • Kal., Īdibus, Nōnīs, fēstus diēs cum erit, corōnam in focum indat

    on the Kalends, the Ides and the Nones, and whenever there is a feast day, she is to put a garland on the hearthCato, Agr. 143.2

  • Sāturnālibus, optimō diērum!

    on the Saturnalia, the best of days!Catull. 14.15

See also holidays, celebrate, anniversary, Christmas, Easter, weekday.
